## Methods

Preparation of CD₃ND₃PbI₃

All starting materials were purchased from Energy Chemical. CD₃ND₂ was obtained by dissolving anhydrous methylamine gas in D₂O. Lead(II) acetate trihydrate was dissolved in D₂O three times to promote H/D exchange and then dried under vacuum. Deuterated hydroiodic acid (DI, 57 wt% in water) was synthesized by reacting 50 wt% hypophosphorous acid–d₃ (in D₂O) with potassium iodide (KI) at 170 °C. The resulting DI vapor was condensed and collected.

For crystal growth54, 1 M solutions of PbI₂ and CD₃ND₃I were prepared separately in γ-butyrolactone (GBL) and heated to 60 °C. The solutions were filtered using a 0.2 μm PTFE syringe filter, and 2 mL of the filtered solution was transferred to a vial and placed in a 110 °C oil bath. Crystals began to appear after ~20 min. The crystals were collected, washed three times with deuterated diethyl ether, and vacuum-dried at room temperature. The synthesized CD₃ND₃PbI₃ was characterized by ¹³C nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, performed on a Bruker Avance 600 MHz NMR spectrometer at 25 °C using deuterated DMSO as the solvent. The methyl carbon peak of CD₃ND₃PbI₃ appears around 23.8 ppm. The multiple splittings of this peak indicate the successful synthesis of the deuterated perovskite CD₃ND₃PbI₃ (Supplementary Fig. 17). The unit cell parameters obtained from single-crystal analysis are listed in Supplementary Table 2.

Preparation of Perovskite Films

The precursor solution was prepared by dissolving methylammonium iodide (MAI) and lead iodide (PbI₂) in a 1:1 molar ratio. The mixture was stirred in N,N-dimethylformamide at 60 °C for 12 hours. The resulting solution was then spin-coated onto glass substrates and subsequently annealed at 120 °C for 25 minutes under a nitrogen atmosphere.

Device fabrication and measurements

Prior to fabrication, the substrates were sequentially cleaned in deionized water, isopropanol, and acetone using ultrasonic treatment for a total duration of one hour. After cleaning, the substrates were dried with a nitrogen flow. Cobalt (Co) bottom electrodes were deposited by high-vacuum electron beam evaporation through a shadow mask at a deposition rate of approximately 1 Å/s. Subsequently, a thin aluminum layer (~1.7 nm) was thermally evaporated at 0.3 Å/s, followed by immediate air plasma oxidation to form a tunneling AlOx layer. Perovskite precursor solutions were spin-coated onto the substrates inside a nitrogen-filled glovebox to achieve films of varying thicknesses. On top of the perovskite layer, a 12 nm NiFe top electrode was deposited using a low-temperature process to minimize damage to the underlying organic layer. The deposition was performed at a rate of 0.7 Å/s with a shadow mask to define the device area, which was approximately 0.2 mm². The thickness of the intermediate layer was determined by spectroscopic ellipsometry (SE-VE-L, Wuhan Eoptics Technology Co., Ltd).

Magnetocurrent measurements were conducted using a vacuum magnetic probe station (CRX-EM-HF, Lake Shore Cryotronics Co., Ltd.) employing a standard four-probe configuration. The spin diffusion length was extracted using the modified Jullière model, described by the following expression:

MC = (IP - IAP) ⁄ IAP = 2P1P2 e-(d-d0)⁄λs ⁄ (1 + P1P2 e-(d-d0)⁄λs) (8)

where d represents the thickness of the organic spacer layer between the ferromagnetic electrodes, and d₀ accounts for the thickness of the ill-defined interfacial region. P₁ and P₂ correspond to the spin polarization at the injection and detection interfaces, respectively.

Cross-sectional high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) samples were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) system (FEI Strata DB235). A 100 nm thick Al protective layer was deposited on top of the devices prior to FIB milling. High-resolution TEM images were acquired using an FEI G2 F30 microscope operated at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV.

Transient Absorption Spectroscopy with Circular Polarization

The transient absorption measurement is based on the femtosecond laser (ORPHEUS-HP, Light Conversion) and the transient absorption spectrometer (HARPIA-TA, Light Conversion). An ultrafast pump laser beam is converted into right or left circularly polarized light by a Berek compensator. A white light probe beam is converted into left circularly polarized light using a linear polarizer and a quarter wave plate.

Transient Reflection Microscopy

Ultrafast transient reflection microscopy was performed using an experimental setup previously constructed by our collaborators. In this setup, a portion of the 800 nm femtosecond laser output was frequency-doubled to 400 nm via a β-Barium borate (BBO) crystal to serve as the pump beam. The probe beam was generated by an optical parametric amplifier (OPA), providing tunable output for selective excitation and detection. The two beams were spatially overlapped on the sample through a custom-built microscope platform, enabling diffraction-limited spatial resolution. Temporal delay between pump and probe pulses was introduced using a motorized delay stage, allowing for time-resolved mapping of the transient optical response.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript reports that efficient room-temperature spin transport in organic-inorganic hybrid perovskite can be achieved through isotope engineering, specifically by substituting hydrogen with deuterium in methylammonium lead iodide to effectively suppress the previously overlooked hyperfine interactions of the organic sublattice. By studying the longitudinal spin lifetime, the magnetocurrent of spin-valve devices, and the spin photovoltaic effect, the authors provided some fundamental understanding of spin relaxation in hybrid materials and established isotope engineering as a powerful strategy to access robust, room-temperature spin functionality. However, the manuscript would benefit from clarifying several uncertain points to support its hypothesized statements.
1. The authors note that although charge carriers mainly propagate within the inorganic Pb–I framework, the hyperfine interaction possesses a long-range character extending beyond 20 Å, which is significantly greater than the ~3 Å separation between the organic cations and the inorganic lattice. While this feature could, in principle, explain how charge carriers couple to the nuclear spins of the organic cations, the manuscript does not clearly elaborate or model how such a long-range HFI dynamically interacts with the rapidly moving spin-polarized carriers in the inorganic backbone, nor does it discuss its relative contribution to established spin-relaxation mechanisms such as the Elliott–Yafet and D’yakonov–Perel’ processes. Moreover, although the authors provide theoretical calculations indicating that deuteration weakens the HFI coupling strength by approximately 6.5 fold, the manuscript does not quantitatively relate this reduction to the observed 2.6 fold increase in spin lifetime. A more detailed quantitative correlation or mechanistic analysis would strengthen the argument and improve the overall clarity of the discussion.
2. The manuscript reports carrier mobility values measured by transient reflection microscopy: 54.5 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ for the non-deuterated material and 51.1 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ for the deuterated counterpart. Although FT-IR and photoluminescence lifetime measurements confirm that deuteration suppresses vibrational frequencies and lowers molecular vibrational energies, the manuscript does not clearly establish how this specific vibrational softening quantitatively or mechanistically translates into enhanced scattering during carrier transport, thereby causing the observed minor decrease in mobility. A more explicit discussion connecting the vibrational changes to charge-transport dynamics would help substantiate this interpretation.
3. The manuscript reports the observation of a room-temperature spin photovoltaic effect and highlights that, by carefully tuning the light intensity and applied bias, the total device current can be adjusted to approaching zero. When the total current approaches zero, the magnetocurrent value tends toward infinity. The manuscript presents this as a potential route toward realizing ultra-low-power spintronic devices; however, it does not further discuss the operational precision required to maintain such an exact zero-current balance, nor the stability and reproducibility of this condition for practical applications.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents the suppression of hyperfine interaction in hybrid perovskites through isotope engineering (H → D substitution), leading to enhanced spin lifetime, improved room-temperature spin transport, and the demonstration of a spin photovoltaic effect (S-PV). The topic is timely and scientifically meaningful; however, several key aspects of the analysis remain largely qualitative, and the physical interpretations rely on descriptive explanations rather than quantitative or model-supported arguments. For publication in Nature Communications, the manuscript requires substantial reinforcement in the following areas.
1. Although the authors extract the longitudinal spin lifetime from transient absorption measurements, the manuscript does not describe how the fitting was performed or what kinetic model was applied. Because spin-lifetime values depend strongly on the functional form used for fitting, omitting this information significantly limits reproducibility and undermines the credibility of the extracted parameters.
Moreover, while the authors estimate the spin diffusion length using the measured lifetime and diffusion parameters, the manuscript does not provide a physical, device-level interpretation of what this means for the present spin-valve structure. Specifically, the manuscript should address how much the increased spin lifetime actually improves spin survival across the perovskite spacer thickness used in the device, and what quantitative advantage deuteration provides under the real operating geometry. Without such analysis, the reader cannot assess the actual impact of isotope substitution on the device performance. So, the authors should improve insufficient description of the spin-lifetime extraction method and incomplete discussion of spin diffusion length.
2. Figure 3 shows that the difference in mobility between the protonated and deuterated samples is extremely small - approximately 6%, well within typical sample-to-sample or measurement variation. Nonetheless, the authors interpret this minor change as evidence for increased scattering due to vibrational suppression. This interpretation is not supported by the magnitude of the observed variation, which is too small to draw conclusions about altered scattering mechanisms.
A more reasonable interpretation is that deuteration has minimal influence on carrier mobility. The manuscript should avoid overstating the physical significance of such a small variation unless statistical evidence (error bars, repeated measurements) is presented to justify it.
3. The spin photovoltaic effect (S-PV) is one of the central claims of this manuscript. However, the explanation provided in Figure 4a is conceptual only, and the manuscript does not present any quantitative model that can logically connect the schematic to the experimental results in Figures 4b, 4c, or 4f.
In particular, the following questions remain unanswered:
- Quantitative analysis about the total current reverse sign as illumination increases?
- Quantitative analysis about that the parallel and antiparallel configurations yield different photovoltages
- Under what specific bias–illumination conditions can the authors tune the output current exactly to zero?
- How much carrier reflection or suppression occurs in the antiparallel configuration, and what determines this magnitude?
All of these effects are described qualitatively but not supported by a quantitative charge-transport or spin-dependent recombination model. For a claim as central as a room-temperature S-PV effect, at least a minimal theoretical framework is required to justify the physical interpretation and distinguish this work from prior studies.
4. The authors argue that the increase in spin lifetime due to deuteration leads to an enhancement in photovoltage and S-PV contrast. However, photovoltaic voltage is influenced by multiple factors - recombination dynamics, interfacial energetics, spin-selective reflection, and charge-transport asymmetry - and the manuscript does not demonstrate how the longer spin lifetime affects these parameters.
In its current form, the manuscript presents the argument in a purely qualitative manner, without explaining the mechanism by which enhanced spin lifetime translates into measurable shifts in photovoltage between the parallel and antiparallel configurations. To claim a fundamentally new S-PV mechanism enabled by isotope engineering, the authors must provide a more rigorous, model-based discussion linking the observed spin dynamics to the photovoltaic response.
This work offers an intriguing direction by combining isotope engineering with perovskite spintronics, and the experimental results are potentially impactful. However, the central claims - particularly those related to spin lifetime extraction, spin diffusion length relevance, spin photovoltaic operation, and the mechanistic role of deuteration - are supported primarily by qualitative descriptions rather than quantitative or model-based analysis.
To meet the standards of Nature Communications, the manuscript requires substantial strengthening of its physical arguments and quantitative justification. A more rigorous analytical framework is essential for clearly establishing the novelty and validity of the reported phenomena.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the authors present compelling and somewhat unexpected results regarding spin transport in hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites (OIHPs). They synthesize both single crystals and thin films of CH3NH3PbI3 and its deuterated analogue (CD3ND3PbI3), and demonstrate that spin transport is dramatically enhanced in the deuterated compound. The structural characterization is thorough and convincingly shows that the two materials are nearly identical from the perspective of crystallography and electronic structure, while their vibrational spectra differ substantially. In addition, the charge-carrier mobility, determined via transient reflectivity microscopy, is comparable in both systems, suggesting similar charge-transport mechanisms.
The authors therefore conclude that spin transport is primarily influenced by hyperfine interactions (HFI) originating from hydrogen nuclei in the organic cation, rather than by differences in structure, defects, or charge mobility. The demonstration of a room-temperature spin photovoltaic effect in deuterated perovskite spin valves adds multifunctionality and further strengthens the significance of the work.
Overall, the manuscript is interesting and the results will likely attract the attention of the Nature Communications readership. However, I have several points that require clarification before the paper can be considered for publication:
1. As the authors themselves note, HFI from hydrogen in OIHPs is typically considered negligible compared to the strong spin–orbit coupling of the Pb–I sublattice, which is thought to dominate spin dephasing. Here, the experimental data clearly show that suppressing HFI via deuteration has a dramatic impact on spin lifetime and spin transport. I think the authors should elaborate—at least qualitatively—on why hydrogen HFI is not overshadowed by SOC-induced mechanisms in this system. A conceptual or semi-quantitative discussion would be helpful, even if tentative.
2. In Fig. 1f,g, the magnetocurrent is presented, but no information is given about the device resistance or RA product. A comment on the absolute device resistance would be important—does deuteration affect the resistance or RA product? Similarly, in Fig. 10c (Supplementary), MC is shown as a function of OIHP thickness. It would be important to show or at least comment on how the resistance evolves with thickness. One would expect a significant increase. Is it the case?
3. The authors estimate the spin diffusion length for the deuterated compound based on tau and D. Can a similar estimate be provided for CH3NH3PbI3?
4. How is the thickness controlled or monitored across samples? Via spin-coating parameters? Profilometry? Ellipsometry? More detail would help assess reproducibility of the thickness-dependent measurements.
5. It is unclear whether the measurements in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 were performed on thin films or single crystals. Since spin dynamics and carrier mobility can differ significantly depending on morphology, the authors should state explicitly which type of sample was used in each measurement.
In summary, I find this to be an interesting piece of work with strong potential impact. Addressing the points above would significantly strengthen the manuscript and improve its clarity.

Thanks very much for reviewer’s comments. To evaluate this effect, we have added additional

54.9 ± 1.1 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ for CH₃NH₃PbI₃ and 51.3 ± 1.6 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ for CD₃ND₃PbI₃. These data

and

Deuteration lowers the vibrational frequencies of the organic cation (as confirmed by our FT-IR

description in the main text (Lines 305–311) and removed the overly strong mechanistic wording,
emphasizing instead that deuteration only weakly affects charge transport.
Question 1-3
The manuscript reports the observation of a room-temperature spin photovoltaic effect and
highlights that, by carefully tuning the light intensity and applied bias, the total device current can
be adjusted to approaching zero. When the total current approaches zero, the magnetocurrent value
tends toward infinity. The manuscript presents this as a potential route toward realizing ultra-low-
power spintronic devices; however, it does not further discuss the operational precision required to
maintain such an exact zero-current balance, nor the stability and reproducibility of this condition
for practical applications.
Answer:
We thank the reviewer for raising the important concern regarding the operational precision
required to achieve and maintain the near-zero current condition. In our spin photovoltaic devices,
the total current is governed by two independently and continuously tunable parameters: the
illumination intensity and the applied bias. In practice, both parameters are precisely controlled
via software, which allows real-time monitoring of the device current. By tracking the current
evolution and iteratively adjusting the bias voltage and light intensity, the device can be
reproducibly tuned into a near-zero current regime. Importantly, an exact zero-current condition is
not strictly required; small deviations still yield strongly enhanced magnetocurrent values, making
the effect experimentally accessible rather than relying on an idealized singular point.
Regarding stability and reproducibility, we emphasize that the key factor for the spin photovoltaic
effect is the stability of spin polarization rather than the photovoltaic response itself. The latter is
an intrinsic property of the perovskite material and remains stable as long as the material does not
undergo degradation. In our manuscript, the spin stability has already been systematically
evaluated through long-term spin-valve measurements. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 10d,
deuterated perovskite spin valves retain over 93% of their magnetocurrent after 100 days and
approximately 75% after 400 days at room temperature, demonstrating excellent long-term spin
stability. This robustness ensures that the spin photovoltaic response, including the near-zero
current operating regime, is stable. In addition, the device shows highly reproducible spin-valve
switching under rapid field modulation over 6,454 cycles, with small fluctuations in both the
parallel and antiparallel current levels (Fig. 1e), supporting robust short-term operational
reproducibility. These results confirm that the proposed electro-optical tuning strategy is
compatible with practical device operation and long-term storage.

Quantitative analysis about that the parallel and antiparallel configurations yield different

Answer:
Thanks very much for reviewer’s comments. During the switching between the parallel and
antiparallel magnetic configurations, the device structure remains unchanged, and the perovskite
layer in the middle experiences no modification. Therefore, the photovoltage remains constant at
18.4 mV. The apparent difference in the photovoltage between the antiparallel and parallel states

reverses, the spin current experiences additional scattering during transport. As a result, a larger

current within the total current; a higher spin-current fraction necessitates a larger compensating
bias. The spin-current fraction is governed by several factors, including the spin polarization of the
ferromagnetic electrodes, the spin-diffusion properties of the transport medium, as well as the spin
lifetime and carrier mobility.

performance, including the Curie temperature and spin polarization of the electrodes, the carrier
mobility and spin relaxation time of the semiconductor, the interfacial spin properties, the applied

asymmetry - and the manuscript does not demonstrate how the longer spin lifetime affects these

Answer:
Thank you for the reviewer’s helpful comment. We apologize that our wording may not have
been sufficiently clear and could have led to this misunderstanding. Our intention is to emphasize
that deuteration enhances the spin lifetime and thereby improves spin-dependent device
performance; we do not mean to claim that deuteration increases the intrinsic photovoltaic voltage.
The measurable photovoltage difference between the parallel and antiparallel magnetic
configurations primarily originates from the magnetocurrent-related voltage component under the
measurement condition, rather than from a genuine change in the built-in photovoltaic voltage.
Therefore, this effect should not be attributed to isotope engineering.
This work offers an intriguing direction by combining isotope engineering with perovskite
spintronics, and the experimental results are potentially impactful. However, the central claims -
particularly those related to spin lifetime extraction, spin diffusion length relevance, spin
photovoltaic operation, and the mechanistic role of deuteration - are supported primarily by
qualitative descriptions rather than quantitative or model-based analysis.
To meet the standards of Nature Communications, the manuscript requires substantial
strengthening of its physical arguments and quantitative justification. A more rigorous analytical
framework is essential for clearly establishing the novelty and validity of the reported phenomena.

In this manuscript, the authors present compelling and somewhat unexpected results regarding
spin transport in hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites (OIHPs). They synthesize both single
crystals and thin films of CH3NH3PbI3 and its deuterated analogue (CD3ND3PbI3), and
demonstrate that spin transport is dramatically enhanced in the deuterated compound. The

mechanisms.
The authors therefore conclude that spin transport is primarily influenced by hyperfine interactions
(HFI) originating from hydrogen nuclei in the organic cation, rather than by differences in
structure, defects, or charge mobility. The demonstration of a room-temperature spin photovoltaic
effect in deuterated perovskite spin valves adds multifunctionality and further strengthens the
significance of the work.
Overall, the manuscript is interesting and the results will likely attract the attention of the Nature
Communications readership. However, I have several points that require clarification before the
paper can be considered for publication:
We thank the reviewer's positive assessment of our work and recommendation for publication.

Question 3-1
As the authors themselves note, HFI from hydrogen in OIHPs is typically considered negligible
compared to the strong spin–orbit coupling of the Pb–I sublattice, which is thought to dominate
spin dephasing. Here, the experimental data clearly show that suppressing HFI via deuteration has
a dramatic impact on spin lifetime and spin transport. I think the authors should elaborate—at least
qualitatively—on why hydrogen HFI is not overshadowed by SOC-induced mechanisms in this
system. A conceptual or semi-quantitative discussion would be helpful, even if tentative.
Answer:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that, in lead-halide perovskites, the
strong Pb–I spin–orbit coupling (SOC) is generally expected to make SOC-driven Elliott–
Yafet/D’yakonov–Perel’ (EY/DP) processes central to spin decay for itinerant carriers (Nat.
Commun. 15, 188 (2024)). Our results do not suggest that hydrogen hyperfine interaction (HFI)
replaces SOC; rather, they indicate that a nuclear-spin-related contribution can remain
experimentally visible in the hybrid system and can be selectively tuned.
A key distinction is that organic–inorganic hybrid perovskites introduce material ingredients that
are absent (or strongly reduced) in fully inorganic analogues. First, hybrids exhibit a soft lattice
and pronounced dynamic disorder/carrier–lattice coupling (Chem 4, 2826–2843 (2018)). Second,
by composition they incorporate organic cations containing abundant ^1H nuclear spins (e.g., MA
= CH₃NH₃⁺ and FA = (NH₂)₂CH⁺), which are absent (or greatly reduced) in fully inorganic lead-
halide perovskites (Nat. Rev. Mater. 1, 15007 (2016)).
In realistic films/devices, carriers are not always purely itinerant in the ideal bulk sense. If injected
electrons/holes (or polarons) have any wavefunction overlap with regions influenced by the
organic sublattice—particularly in localized/trapped/polaronic states near interfaces—hyperfine
fields can become non-negligible. In such situations, the apparent DP/EY relaxation can be
partially masked, and the measured decay time can reflect an effective depolarization time that
also involves trapping/detrapping dynamics and inhomogeneous broadening.
